prompt.context: Your client is a large pharmaceutical drug company working on a vaccine for chicken pox. The vaccine needs to pass three phases of testing to be approved by the FDA. It has just completed the second phase and the client is asking your help to decide if they should fund the third phase. The third phase would last 2 years, cost $300M, and results from previous phases indicate the vaccine has a 95% chance of approval. We would be able to start producing vaccine immediately following approval.
prompt.question: Should the client fund the third and final phase of testing for the chicken pox vaccine? (Go / No-Go decision)

clarifying_info.q: What form does the vaccine take?

clarifying_info.a: We are only worried about the US market in this case.

clarifying_info.q: What is the US population and age distribution?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the US population is 300M and uniformly distributed from age 0 to 75 — as many people enter the population as leave every year.

clarifying_info.q: What portion of the population would need the vaccine?
clarifying_info.a: [Hand the candidate Exhibit 1 — cumulative distribution of chicken pox exposure by age.]

clarifying_info.q: How long would it take to vaccinate the existing population?
clarifying_info.a: It is estimated that it would take 3 years to vaccinate the existing population.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of the vaccine?
clarifying_info.a: [Have the candidate estimate the price from Exhibit 2 — willingness to pay chart.]

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs per pill?
clarifying_info.a: Distribution: $1.50; Production: $2.50; SG&A: $5.00. The $300M Phase 3 cost covers everything else (plant setup, etc.) and can be spread over the 2 years of testing.
No, the vaccine will not be patented.

clarifying_info.q: Are other companies working on a similar vaccine?
clarifying_info.a: Other companies would have to undergo the same series of testing. No other companies have started formal testing of the vaccine. Phase 1 and 2 combined take 3 years, giving us 3 years of competitive protection. Phase 1 and 2 cost $200M.

exhibits.title: Cumulative Distribution of Chicken Pox Exposure
exhibits.shows: A curve showing the cumulative percentage of the population that has been exposed to chicken pox by age, from age 0 to 21+
exhibits.data: At age 0: ~0%; rises steeply; reaches approximately 50% by age 9; reaches approximately 100% by age 18-21

exhibits.title: Parent's Willingness to Pay
exhibits.shows: A step-down chart showing the percentage of parents willing to purchase the vaccine at various price points
exhibits.data: 100% willing at ~$10; 75% willing at ~$30; 50% willing at ~$35; 25% willing at ~$40; drops to near 0 above ~$40

framework: Structure the market into two segments: existing population (one-time opportunity) and new babies born each year (ongoing)
Estimate market size for each segment using population data, exposure data from Exhibit 1, and willingness-to-pay from Exhibit 2
Determine optimal price using Exhibit 2 to maximize profit per pill
Build a revenue and cost model by year to project cash flows
Assess NPV at a reasonable pharma hurdle rate, factoring in 95% probability of approval
Evaluate competitive landscape: barriers to entry, timing protection, competitor incentive to enter

questions.prompt: How large is the existing population that needs the vaccine at launch?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 1 shows ~50% of people aged 0-18 have NOT been exposed by age 9 on average, meaning roughly half of ages 0-18 need the vaccine. US population is uniform 0-75, so 300M/75 = 4M people per age cohort. Ages 0-18 = 19 cohorts but the casebook simplifies: 4M * 18 / 2 = 36M people in the existing unvaccinated population 0-18. At 75% willing to pay, that is 36M * 0.75 = 27M vaccines sold over 3 years = 9M per year.

math.setup: US population uniform 0-75: 300M / 75 = 4M per age group. Exhibit 1 implies half of ages 0-18 need vaccine. Annual new baby cohort: 4M. Willingness to pay at $30: 75%.
steps: Willing to purchase: 36M * 75% = 27M over 3 years = 9M per year for years 1-3
New babies per year: 4M * 75% = 3M per year ongoing
math.answer: 9M existing population vaccines/year for 3 years; 3M new baby vaccines/year thereafter

questions.prompt: What price should the client charge for the vaccine?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 2 shows a willingness-to-pay curve. At $30, 75% of parents are willing to buy. Profit = (price - cost per pill). Cost per pill = $1.50 + $2.50 + $5.00 = $9.00. At $30: profit = $21/pill. Candidates should compare revenue * margin at different price points; $30 maximizes expected profit given the drop-off in demand above $30.

math.setup: Cost per pill = $1.50 (distribution) + $2.50 (production) + $5.00 (SG&A) = $9.00. Check profit at $30 vs higher prices using demand from Exhibit 2.
steps: At $30: 75% willing to buy → profit per pill = $30 - $9 = $21
At $35: ~50% willing → profit per pill = $26; but volume drops significantly
math.answer: Recommended price: $30 per pill; profit margin = $21 per pill

questions.prompt: Build a cash flow model by year. What does the revenue and profit picture look like?
questions.guidance: Years 1-3: sell 12M total vaccines (9M existing pop + 3M babies). Year 4 onward: sell 3M vaccines/year (babies only). Phase 3 costs of $300M are spread over 2 years of testing BEFORE launch (years -2 and -1), so they appear as -$150M/year in years 1-2 against revenues or can be treated as pre-launch costs. The table in the casebook offsets them against net in years 1-2.

math.setup: Revenue = vaccines sold * $30. Cost = vaccines sold * $9. Phase 3 cost = $150M/year in years 1-2 (pre-launch or offset). Build annual cash flows.
steps: Year 1: 12M vaccines * $30 = $360M revenue; 12M * $9 = $108M variable cost; net before phase cost = $252M; minus $150M phase 3 = $102M (casebook shows -$150 in testing years separately, netting to $252M in production year 1)
Year 2: same as year 1 = $252M net (after phase cost allocation)
Phase 3 cost: -$150M in each of 2 testing years
math.answer: Net: -$150M, -$150M (testing), then $252M, $252M, $252M, $63M, $63M, ... (millions). High positive NPV at any reasonable pharma discount rate.

questions.prompt: Should phase 3 sunk costs (phases 1 and 2: $200M) factor into this decision?
questions.guidance: No. Phases 1 and 2 costs ($200M) are sunk and should NOT be included in the Go/No-Go NPV calculation. However, they ARE relevant when evaluating whether competitors would rationally choose to enter — competitors would need to spend $200M in phases 1-2 before they could even start competing.

questions.prompt: What is the competitive threat? Should we worry about other companies entering this market?
questions.guidance: Key insight: the vaccine is not patented, but competitors face a natural 3-year barrier because they must complete the same phase 1+2 testing (3 years, $200M). By the time a competitor could launch, our client will have vaccinated the entire existing unvaccinated population (the large one-time opportunity of 27M). After year 3, the market shrinks to just 3M babies/year. A competitor entering at year 6 would only share 3M vaccines/year, and would need to recoup $200M (phases 1-2) + $300M (phase 3) = $500M in total testing costs from a shrinking market. Competitors have little financial incentive to enter.

math.setup: Competitor revenue after entry: share of 3M vaccines/year at $30. Total competitor testing cost: $500M ($200M phases 1-2 + $300M phase 3).
steps: Post-year-3 market: 3M vaccines/year, shared between competitors
Payback on $500M at $31.5M/year = ~16 years — not attractive
math.answer: Competitors have very little incentive to enter. Our client captures the high-value existing population segment exclusively.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should be considered in assessing the overall attractiveness of funding phase 3?

categories.name: Market size and demand
ideas: Existing unvaccinated population (0-18) is a large one-time opportunity
Annual baby cohort provides steady long-term demand
Willingness to pay at 75% at $30 is strong
Market confined to US per case scope

categories.name: Financial attractiveness
ideas: High positive NPV at any reasonable discount rate
$300M phase 3 cost is recovered quickly given volume
5% failure risk reduces expected value but does not materially change Go/No-Go
Phase 1+2 sunk costs should not be included in this decision

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: No patent, but 3-year natural barrier due to FDA testing requirements
Post-year-3 market is small and unattractive for new entrants
First-mover captures the bulk of market value

categories.name: Risk factors
ideas: 5% chance of FDA rejection after $300M spend
Potential price pressure if public health bodies negotiate
Execution risk in scaling production within 2 years

recommendation: The client should fund the third phase of testing (GO decision)
NPV analysis shows high positive returns: ~$252M/year net for 3 years after launch, declining to ~$63M/year — well above the $300M phase 3 investment
Competitive analysis shows virtually no threat: natural 3-year barrier + unattractive post-year-3 economics deter competitors
risks: 5% probability of FDA rejection, resulting in loss of $300M phase 3 investment
If the vaccine is not adopted at sufficient rates, revenue projections fall short
Unexpected competitive entry, though assessed as unlikely
next_steps: Proceed with phase 3 funding immediately to preserve 3-year competitive window
Begin production planning and distribution partnerships to minimize time-to-market post-approval
Monitor for any competitor announcements of phase 1 testing initiation
